idiom_name: switch expression with type patterns over a sealed interface
implementation_notes: Modern C# makes the operation a function over a closed type set: declare the nodes as records implementing a sealed interface and write each operation as a switch expression with type patterns. Adding an operation is a new method and never edits the nodes; the compiler warns when a switch expression does not cover every possible input, and a sealed hierarchy is what makes that warning meaningful. The classic accept()/visit() structure is still the right shape when the nodes come from a library you do not own (Roslyn ships exactly that), when operations must be enumerable or loadable as types (reflection over ICartVisitor implementations in a plugin host), or when an operation needs many methods and shared per-instance state.
pitfalls: Exhaustiveness is checked per switch expression at the position where it is written: add a record subtype and the build only fails in the files that contain the switch - run the full solution, not just the changed project.
A silent default arm (returning 0 or an empty list) converts a missing case into a wrong answer; make the discard arm throw.
Type patterns use runtime type tests, so an implicit conversion or a base-class arm placed first can shadow a more specific arm.
Records give value equality and init-only properties, which is exactly what a pattern-matched hierarchy wants; using mutable classes instead invites a visitor that mutates nodes mid-switch.

variants.name: Subclass the framework's visitor (Roslyn CSharpSyntaxVisitor / CSharpSyntaxWalker)
variants.implementation_notes: When the element hierarchy belongs to a framework, use the visitor the framework already ships instead of inventing one: CSharpSyntaxVisitor declares Visit(node) plus one virtual VisitX method per node type with a DefaultVisit fallback, and CSharpSyntaxWalker adds depth-first descent through nodes, tokens and trivia (and a recursion-depth guard) for you. This is the classic GoF structure maintained by the platform, with the classic cost: every new C# language construct adds a Visit method, which is why unhandled cases fall back to DefaultVisit instead of breaking existing subclasses - the same mitigation the JDK uses with AbstractElementVisitor. Use CSharpSyntaxRewriter, not the visitor, when the operation must change the tree.
pitfalls: Forgetting base.VisitX(node) in an override stops the walk at that node and silently misses every descendant.
CSharpSyntaxWalker descends tokens and trivia according to its depth setting; pick SyntaxWalkerDepth deliberately or the operation sees less or more than intended.
Syntax trees are immutable - a visitor that must rewrite code needs CSharpSyntaxRewriter (or a separate rewriter pass) rather than mutating nodes.
Deep trees can overflow the stack; the walker guards against that internally, but visitor code that recurses on its own must do the same.
